subject: Copywriting
title: John Caples: Testing Headlines
description: Learn John Caples: Testing Headlines in one minute.

hook.text: 'They Laughed When I Sat Down at the Piano—But When I Started to Play!' John Caples wrote the most famous headline ever.

buildup.text: Caples worked at BBDO and became the master of direct response ads that measured every dollar spent against dollars.

discovery.text: His book 'Tested Advertising Methods' catalogued which headline formulas worked and which flopped, proven by data.

twist.text: Caples proved changing just the headline could multiply response rates by 19x. Everything else—same copy, same product.

climax.text: The annual Caples Awards honor him. Every A/B test in digital marketing is Caples' legacy, digitized.

punchline.text: One headline, 19x more sales. Caples proved words pay.

quiz.question: By how much could a headline change multiply response rates according to Caples?

details.summary: John Caples wrote 'They Laughed When I Sat Down at the Piano — But When I Started to Play!' in 1926, creating one of the most famous headlines in advertising history. He spent his career scientifically testing headlines and proved that changing a headline alone could multiply response rates...
details.whyItMatters: Caples proved with data that the headline is the most important element in any ad. His testing methodology laid the groundwork for modern A/B testing and conversion optimization.
takeaways: His piano headline is one of the most copied formats in advertising history
Headline changes alone could increase response rates by 2,000%
He brought scientific rigor to creative copywriting decisions
keywords: They Laughed When I Sat Down

faq.question: Why is the piano headline so legendary?
faq.answer: It tells a mini-story in one sentence, creates curiosity, involves social drama, and promises transformation. The 'They Laughed... But...' formula has been imitated thousands of times because it instantly engages the reader's emotions and curiosity.

faq.question: How did Caples test his headlines?
faq.answer: Caples ran split tests in newspapers and magazines, measuring actual response rates — coupons returned, orders placed — rather than opinions. This empirical approach proved that specific, benefit-driven headlines dramatically outperformed clever or vague ones.
